# Introduction {.unnumbered}

This book follows one experiment: growing a brain in a simulation, one piece at a time, in roughly the order in
which brains are thought to have evolved.

Each stage adds a small circuit to the brain of the previous stage and changes the world so that the new circuit
has something to be good for. Evolution then gets a number of generations to put the circuit to use. A page of
this book is the report of one stage: what was added and why, the biology it is modelled on, and what happened.

## The animals and their world

The animals live on a grid. Each has a stomach that empties a little every tick (one tick is about a second of
behaviour) and faster when it moves. An animal whose stomach is empty dies. Food grows on bushes; an eaten bush
regrows after a while.

The objects, their names and their pictures come from the game *One Hour One Life*. The simulation uses a small
slice of the game's rules at each stage and a larger one as the brain grows.

An animal senses the world through a few coarse "eyes": a handful of directions, in each of which it sees whether
something is there, how near it is, and what it looks like. What something looks like is a short list of numbers,
its *appearance*. It can step forward, turn left or right, and grasp what is in front of it.

## The brain

The brain is a network of model neurons. A neuron has an activity between 0 and 1 and passes it on through
synapses, each with a strength. A neuron is either excitatory (it raises the activity of the neurons it reaches)
or inhibitory (it lowers it), never both. Neurons are grouped into *regions*, and a *projection* is the set of
synapses from one region to another.

Some projections are **evolved**: which synapses exist and how strong they are is inherited, with mutations, and
shaped by selection. Others are **hard-wired**: they are designed, and evolution can only make the whole
projection stronger or weaker. A hard-wired projection gives a group of neurons a fixed meaning, such as "this
hurts", that later stages can build on.

## How evolution runs

A population is 64 genomes. Each genome lives as four siblings in a shared world, once. The genomes that did best
have children, each from two parents, with a few mutations. That is one generation.

**Fitness** is what selection rewards. Here it is the *well-fed lifetime*: how long the animal lived, counted
from its first meal, with each tick weighted by how full its stomach was. An animal that never eats scores zero.

## How a stage is judged

One life is mostly luck, and one evolution run can end almost anywhere. So every stage is run three times with
different random seeds, and every result is given as a mean with its standard error over those seeds.

Each stage has a **main** run, with the new circuit, and a **control**: the brain of the previous stage in the
same new world, starting from the same population. The new circuit is then the only difference between them.

A stage succeeds when two things hold:

1. **The circuit is used.** The final population is put back in its world with the new neurons silenced. If the
   animals do clearly worse without them, in every seed, they were using them. This is called a *lesion* test.
2. **Main is not worse than control.** It does not have to be better. The point of a stage is a circuit that
   later stages can build on.

A circuit that is not used is left out of the brain, and the page says so.

## How to read a stage page

Every page has the same parts: the idea and its biology, the circuit as a diagram, the results, and the list of
runs behind them, with a link to a *dashboard* that replays the last generation of a run. Where it helps, a page
zooms in on one animal over a few dozen ticks, so that you can watch the circuit work.

The numbers, graphs and diagrams are drawn from data files that are written when a stage is run. Only the text
is written by hand.
